How Fast Do Unit Distances Grow?

LimitsNumber TheoryUnit Distance Problem
Game: Watch how many pairs the best grid can have as the number of points grows, and compare it with the straight lines that mark the known limits.
How to play: Slide the grid size. The purple line is the best grid, the dashed curve is a limit that no arrangement can beat, and the thin lines show different growth speeds.

Look for the math

Write u(n) for the most unit distances among n points of the plane. Nobody knows u(n) exactly. The chart shows what is known, with both axes on a log scale so that growth like ns is a straight line of slope s.

The grid: slope barely above 1

The purple line is the best k × k grid (the best spacing for each k), and it is real data, computed here. The exponent log(pairs)/log(n) is about 1.15 at 16 points, 1.24 at 256 and 1.25 at 4,096. Erdős's formula says it creeps towards 1 + C/log log n, and at sizes anyone can draw that is far from a straight line. The article's example: a 1,296-point grid has 7,632 unit pairs, and the test reproduces this number.

The ceiling: slope 4/3

The dashed curve is the ceiling from the previous page, which is a proof valid for every n. The best proved ceiling, from the crossing number inequality, has slope 4/3, and it is drawn here only as a guide, since its constant is not shown.

The new line: slope 1.014

For decades the conjecture was that u(n) is n1 + o(1), a slope that tends to 1. In 2026 an OpenAI model found a construction that disproved it, and Will Sawin's clean-up proves at least n1.014 unit pairs for large n. That is the third guide line. The gap between 1.014 and 4/3 is still open. The guide lines start at the same point and show slopes only. The new construction does not win at sizes you can draw: the effect is for huge n.

Slide to 64. Does the purple line look straighter than the slope-1 line? What would you need to see to tell 1.014 from 1?
